q: Which area of a house best suits rubber flooring?
n: Rubber flooring is resilient, so it cushions falls and is quiet underfoot. That makes it ideal for a child's playroom. Source: Resilient Floor Covering Institute; Ching, Interior Design Illustrated.

q: Which flooring suits clients who want a sustainable option?
n: Linoleum is made of natural, renewable materials (linseed oil, cork and wood flour, jute backing) and is biodegradable, a sustainable flooring choice. Source: Resilient Floor Covering Institute; LEED materials guidance.

q: Which room is most appropriate for carpet flooring?
n: Carpet absorbs sound and footfall noise and controls reflections, which suits a home theater where quiet and good acoustics matter most. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics; Carpet and Rug Institute acoustic data.

q: If ease of replacement and affordability are priorities, which flooring is most suitable?
n: Vinyl tiles are among the cheapest resilient floors, and a damaged tile can be pulled up and replaced individually. Source: Resilient Floor Covering Institute; local supplier price lists.

q: Which flooring has pigment through its full thickness, not just at the surface?
n: Homogeneous vinyl has the same composition and pigment through its full thickness, so wear does not change its look. Printed vinyl and laminate carry the design only on a surface layer. Source: ASTM F1913 (vinyl sheet without backing); manufacturer literature.

q: What is the rate at which acoustic energy is radiated, in watts?
n: Sound power is the total acoustic energy a source radiates per unit time, measured in watts. Sound pressure (pascals or dB) is what is measured at a point. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics; Long, Architectural Acoustics.

q: What is the sound level at which sound becomes painful?
n: The threshold of pain is the sound level at which hearing becomes painful, about 120–130 dB. The threshold of audibility is 0 dB. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics.

q: What branch of physics studies sound, its behavior and control?
n: Acoustics is the branch of physics dealing with the production, transmission, behavior and control of sound. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics.

q: What is the unit of loudness level?
n: The phon is the unit of loudness level: a sound's loudness in phons equals the dB level of a 1,000 Hz tone judged equally loud. Source: ISO 226 (equal-loudness contours); Egan, Architectural Acoustics.

q: What is the lowest frequency in a complex tone?
n: The fundamental is the lowest frequency in a complex tone. The harmonics (overtones) are whole-number multiples of it. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics.

q: If a wall's transmission coefficient is 0.001, what is its transmission loss?
n: TL = 10 log (1/τ) = 10 log (1/0.001) = 10 log 1,000 = 30 dB. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics (transmission loss).

q: Which of these does NOT significantly affect sound transmission between rooms?
n: Sound transmission depends mainly on the partition: its mass, thickness, area, construction and airtightness. The room's size has only a minor effect. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics; ASTM E90/E413.

q: What happens to sound in a long and narrow hallway?
o: Sound will be absorbed by the ceiling
Sound will be absorbed by the floor
Sound will bounce back and forth more rapidly
n: In a long, narrow hallway the walls are close and parallel, so sound reflects back and forth between them rapidly, causing flutter and a lively, noisy space. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics.

q: What is the persistence of sound by repeated reflection after the source stops?
n: Reverberation is the persistence of sound in a room from many repeated reflections after the source stops. It is measured as reverberation time (RT60). Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics; Sabine's formula.

q: What is the rapid, repeated reflection between parallel hard surfaces that sounds like fluttering?
n: Flutter echo is a rapid series of reflections between two parallel hard surfaces, heard as a buzzing or fluttering. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics.

q: For amusic hall with a large audience, what is the most appropriate flooring material?
n: Wood planks are durable under a large audience and give music halls a warm, resonant floor that supports the sound rather than deadening it like carpet. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics; Beranek, Concert Halls and Opera Houses.

q: An office manager wants to see into the adjacent music room. Which partition is best acoustically?
n: A heavy 150 mm CHB wall with fixed (sealed) glazing gives the most mass and no operable gaps, so it blocks the most sound while keeping the view. Lightweight board and sliding glass leak more. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics (mass law); ASTM E413 (STC).

q: What is the most effective way to reduce airborne sound transmission?
n: Absorptive materials, in the partition cavity and on room surfaces, convert sound energy to heat, reducing the airborne sound that builds up and passes to adjoining spaces. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics.

q: Which of the following is the most effective method for preventing sound transmission between rooms?
n: A double wall on separate studs or leaves with a cavity breaks the structural path for vibration, giving much higher sound insulation than a single wall of the same mass. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics; ASTM E413 (STC of double walls).

q: Which element mainly controls how much sound is reflected within a room?
n: The wall surfaces' treatment (absorptive or reflective, flat or diffusing) mainly decides how much sound is reflected within the room. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics.

q: What is the best ceiling material when considering acoustic performance?
n: Gypsum board ceilings, especially perforated acoustic gypsum with backing, give good acoustic performance. Gypsum is also light and fire-resistant. Source: Gypsum Association; manufacturer acoustic data (USG Boral).

q: Which shape is best avoided in room design to prevent undesirable sound focusing and echo?
n: A dome's concave surface focuses reflected sound at points, creating hot spots and echoes, so it is the shape most to be avoided acoustically. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics (concave surfaces).

q: Which wall material best cuts echo in a recording studio?
n: Open-cell acoustic foam absorbs mid and high frequencies, cutting echo and flutter in recording studios. Glass and concrete reflect sound. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics; ASTM C423 (sound absorption).

q: In acoustic design, what does STC measure?
o: How well a partition blocks sound
n: STC (Sound Transmission Class) is a single-number rating of how well a partition blocks airborne sound. Higher means better isolation. Source: ASTM E413 (classification for rating sound insulation).

q: Which material is commonly used on ceilings and walls to absorb sound?
n: Acoustic boards are porous or perforated panels with high absorption (NRC), used on ceilings and walls to absorb sound. Source: ASTM C423 / NRC ratings; manufacturer literature.

q: A manager wants cubicle partitions that help acoustics yet keep visual contact. What fits?
o: Low modular partitions with a glass strip in the middle
n: Low modular partitions with fabric-covered absorptive panels reduce noise between cubicles, and a glass strip keeps visual contact. Source: ASTM E1374 (open office acoustics); Egan, Architectural Acoustics.

q: What material is best used on walls to reduce sound transmission?
n: A gypsum board on stud assembly, especially with insulation in the cavity, forms a mass–spring–mass system that reduces sound transmission efficiently for its weight. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics; Gypsum Association GA-600 (STC ratings).

q: Which part of a door should be treated first to cut sound transmission?
n: Sound leaks most through gaps, so a door's perimeter edges should be sealed first (gaskets, door bottoms). Even a solid leaf performs poorly if its edges leak. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics; ASTM E1408 (door sound transmission).

q: Which inexpensive yet effective wall treatment would you recommend to reduce noise?
n: Egg-crate (profiled) acoustic foam is a cheap, easily installed wall treatment that absorbs mid- and high-frequency sound and reduces echo. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics; ASTM C423.

q: Which floor finish best reduces noise in an office?
n: Carpet tiles absorb footfall and airborne noise, so offices are quieter than with hard floors. Source: Carpet and Rug Institute acoustic data; Egan, Architectural Acoustics.

q: Which type of flooring is made from polymers?
n: Resilient flooring (vinyl, VCT, rubber, linoleum) is made from polymers and is elastic, recovering from indentation. Source: Resilient Floor Covering Institute.

q: Which facility suits rubber flooring best?
n: Rubber flooring cushions impact, gives grip and resists heavy wear and dropped weights, so it suits sports halls and gyms. Source: Resilient Floor Covering Institute; ASTM F2772 (sports floors).

q: If low maintenance and ease of replacement are priorities for a high-end project, which flooring should be specified?
n: Luxury carpet tiles give a high-end look with low maintenance, and single damaged tiles can be lifted and replaced without redoing the floor. Source: Carpet and Rug Institute; manufacturer literature (Interface).

q: For maximum durability in any condition, easy installation, and the longest lifespan, which flooring should be specified?
n: Ceramic and porcelain tile is very hard, waterproof and stain- and fire-resistant, installs simply and lasts the longest in almost any condition. Source: TCNA Handbook; ANSI A137.1.

q: Which resilient flooring is made from renewable materials?
n: Cork is the bark of the cork oak, harvested every 9–10 years without felling the tree, so cork tile is a renewable resilient flooring. Source: Resilient Floor Covering Institute; LEED materials guidance.

q: What is the best acoustic treatment location for narrow spaces?
n: In narrow spaces the walls are close and parallel and cause flutter echo, so treating the walls is the most effective first step. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics.

q: In asmall conference room, where should acoustic panels primarily be placed to reduce echo?
n: In a small conference room the ceiling is the largest reflecting surface between talkers, so acoustic panels there control echo most effectively. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics; ANSI S12.60 (classroom acoustics principles).

q: Where are acoustic baffles most effective in a large open-plan office?
n: In a large open-plan office, baffles hung from the ceiling absorb sound over the whole floor area and cut reflections between workstations. Source: ASTM E1374; Egan, Architectural Acoustics.

q: Where should acoustic treatment be concentrated in a home theater?
n: In a home theater, the early reflections that blur sound come off the side and rear walls, so acoustic treatment is concentrated there. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics; CEDIA home theater design guidelines.

q: In a tall lobby full of hard surfaces, where should absorption go first?
n: A tall lobby's ceiling is the largest free hard surface, often the only one not taken by glass, doors or floor finishes, so it is where absorption goes first. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics.
